title: Digital Independence Day: Messaging your audience
content:
As an organisation, you want to be easy to reach for your target group or audience. That’s why many organisations use messaging apps, alongside being reachable by phone or email. But that’s not their only function: messaging is also widely used for collaboration and for maintaining communities.

Mention messaging, and many people immediately think of WhatsApp. With more than 13 million users in the Netherlands, it’s the most widely used communication app and, for many people, the platform for staying in touch. Unfortunately, using WhatsApp does come with some downsides. WhatsApp is owned by Meta, the company that’s also behind Facebook and Instagram. Meta’s main business model is selling personalised advertising, and to do that as effectively as possible, it wants to collect as much information as possible about everyone. Messages in one-to-one chats are encrypted by default, so Meta can’t easily read along, but that protection isn’t there for group chats or chats linked to a helpdesk or support system. And even without reading the messages, Meta can infer all kinds of personal information from usage data.

So this month, we’re looking at alternatives for: chat tools.

title: Digital Independence Day: Getting started with web analytics
content:
The holidays are behind us again, so it’s time to take a look at how your website has performed over the past month. Chances are you’ll be diving into the latest Google Analytics reports to do that.

Google Analytics has been the standard tool for web analytics for years. Because Google offers the tool for free to most people, it has become deeply rooted in the web. Around 83% of websites that track statistics do so with Google Analytics (that’s almost 48% of all websites). An incredible market share, then.

What many people (apparently) don’t realise is that by installing Google Analytics on their website, they’re handing their visitors’ browsing data to Google on a silver platter. And although you can strip down the tracker considerably so that it sends as little personal data as possible (which keeps you just within the GDPR rules, without having to ask for consent), you’re still giving Google a huge advantage in learning as much as possible about visitors and their behaviour.

So it’s time to break that monopoly and get started with the alternatives.

title: Digital Independence Day: Getting started with language models
content:
These days, you can’t read a newspaper or newsletter without being flooded with articles about AI and how big and important these developments are. Huge investments, geopolitical interests, the impact on our lives and on the planet: sometimes it seems as if everything revolves around AI these days. That’s why, as part of Digital Independence Day, we’re turning our sights this Sunday to the world of AI and language models in the workplace.

Because in our daily work, too, AI is increasingly being pushed on us. If your organisation uses Microsoft 365, you can now ‘oh-so-easily’ use Copilot, Microsoft’s AI assistant, in almost all its products. And if you haven’t tried it yourself yet, you probably have colleagues who eagerly use ChatGPT or Claude. To write a summary or a translation, for example, or perhaps a first draft of a presentation? And do we still need that expensive illustrator if we can just ‘generate’ an image? (Editor’s note: the illustrations for this series are made by a real human being!)

title: Digital Independence Day: Switch to alternative form services
content:
Organising an event and want to know whether potential participants are coming and if they have any dietary requirements? Or running an open call where makers can apply with their email address, phone number and a motivation letter as an attachment? Online form tools such as Google Forms are often used for this. But which tool do you choose if you don’t want to rely on a big tech company? And how do you make sure your audience’s data stays safe?

Many organisations use Microsoft Office 365 or Google Workspace in the office. Both platforms also include a tool for creating your own forms. And what makes these tools ridiculously handy on top of that is that the results flow into an online spreadsheet in real time, where you can immediately run your analyses. Still, there are major objections to using these two companies’ forms.

title: Digital Independence Day: Switch to alternative video platforms
content:
Teachers, marketers and communications professionals often share videos with their network or audience. From promotional videos to conference recordings, educational videos and tutorials. For many, YouTube is the most obvious option. It’s easy, cheap and everyone knows it. But of course, using YouTube to host your videos comes with major problems. So this week: alternatives to YouTube during Digital Independence Day.

So what are the downsides of YouTube? First of all: YouTube collects data on your audience’s behaviour. If you send a link to the children in your class or the people in your network, you’re forcing them to hand over their data to YouTube. And that’s before we even get to the persistent algorithms, which are used, among other things, to suggest what to watch next once the video ends. Before you know it, they’ve fallen down some rabbit hole. It all makes sense once you look into YouTube’s business model: get people to spend as much time on YouTube as possible, and sell as many ads as possible. A model that, as we now know, encourages nasty, addictive and opaque practices.

title: Digital Independence Day: Switch to alternative video calling services
content:
Still using Zoom, Google Meet or Microsoft Teams in your organisation? Then it’s worth considering a switch to an autonomous, privacy-friendly tool. On this Digital Independence Day, we give you an overview of the downsides of the current big tech video calling providers, and a list of great alternatives.

Digital Independence Day takes place every first Sunday of the month. It’s an initiative recently launched in Germany by the Chaos Computer Club and Save Social, together with a large group of German organisations. The day is all about switching to privacy-friendly alternatives to big tech, making your organisation less dependent on big tech software services.

On the agenda this Sunday: online meeting tools and video conferencing tools.

Whether it’s for a meeting, a webinar or a gathering of your community: video calling is personal, easy and quick. Many organisations still use Google Meet or Microsoft Teams for video calls. These applications are often already available in the work environment and are simple to use. But: all three of these big tech tools come from the United States, they’re not very transparent, and the companies behind them hold enormous monopolistic market power.

title: Digital Independence Day: Switch to alternative newsletter services
content:
Organisations rely heavily on big tech services and software, such as Google Drive, Microsoft Office and social media platforms like Instagram and YouTube. For a long time, hardly anyone batted an eye. But in times of geopolitical unrest and a worrying dependence on American and Chinese big tech companies, the importance of using safe and independent technology is now widely recognised.

That’s why more and more organisations want to break away from big tech. But how do you go about it? PublicSpaces supports public and civil society organisations in becoming digitally autonomous, step by step. And because we like to share what we know, we’re joining the ‘Digital Independence Day’ initiative, recently launched in Germany by the Chaos Computer Club and Save Social together with a large group of German organisations.

Every first Sunday of the month is Digital Independence Day: a day dedicated to making the switch to privacy-friendly alternatives to big tech as easy as possible! Each month, PublicSpaces discusses alternatives that make your organisation less dependent on big tech software services. On this first Sunday of March, we’re looking at newsletter applications.

title: Letter to the Dutch House of Representatives: protect European organisations against foreign sanctions pressure
content:
On 17 September 2026, PublicSpaces and 37 organisations sent a joint letter to the House of Representatives and the Cabinet. The call: protect European organisations and their users against foreign sanctions pressure, now that US sanctions are increasingly hitting innocent European parties too.

Freedom of expression, freedom of the press and freedom of printing have been enshrined in the Dutch Constitution since 1848. A democratic state under the rule of law can only function if these freedoms are properly safeguarded. That is why it is worrying that the US government is using sanctions to silence ideological opponents. Sometimes it does so directly, as with the judges of the International Criminal Court, and sometimes indirectly, as with the internet service Autistici/Inventati (A/I).

title: Save the date: PublicSpaces Conference 2026 on june 4, 5 & 6
content:
The sixth edition of the PublicSpaces conference focuses on the impact of technology on our democracy.

Whereas in its early days the internet was seen as a great promise for our democracy—giving everyone a voice and providing unlimited access to information—today it is seen above all as a threat. The digital space is dominated by big tech companies whose primary goal is to maximize profits. The internet increasingly serves as an arena for geopolitical strategies. Non-transparent algorithms and the unrestrained spread of AI-generated fake news cause disinformation and polarization. As a result, a shared reality—with room for democratic values such as freedom of expression, the prohibition of discrimination, and the right to privacy—is no longer a given, and public debate and free elections are under threat.
snippet: The sixth edition of the PublicSpaces conference focuses on the impact of technology on our democracy.
creator: Laura Krabbe

title: Join the Watch Party Data Morgana: Episode 1 ‘The Online Public Space’
content:
The internet has fallen into the hands of a few Big Tech companies. With the promise to make our world better, fairer, and more efficient, they are collecting our data on a huge scale. Has this really made the world a better place, or is that merely an illusion – a ‘Data Morgana’?

Our dependency on Big Tech raises more and more concern now that both Meta and X abolished moderation on their platforms, and are mingling with politics – both in the US and in Europe. Can we break loose of this dependency? In the ‘Data Morgana’ talkshow, we engage in conversation with experts, scientists, artists and entrepreneurs to shape a better future for our internet.

On Monday, March 24, at 8:00 PM CET, we are hosting the first watch party of episode 1 of Data Morgana via the journalistic platform Display Europe! Afterwards, there will be room for discussion.
